summary.text: Partition the integers into blocks \(100q\le n<100q+100\): whenever the digit sum of \(q\) exceeds a fixed threshold, the nine offsets \(9,19,\ldots,89\) all give value \(8\), while any fixed \(m\ne8\) can occur at most once in the block. Prefixes with bounded digit sum have density zero (their number grows only polynomially in the number of digits), so the limiting upper frequency of every \(m\ne8\) is at most \(1/100\), whereas that of \(8\) is at least \(9/100\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S(n)=\text{the sum of the decimal digits of }n,
\qquad
a(n)=S(n)\bmod S(n+1),
\]
and, for \(m,N\in\mathbb N\), let
\[
A_m(N)=\#\{0\le n<N:a(n)=m\}.
\]
We prove that for every \(m\),
\[
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{A_m(N)}N
\le
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{A_8(N)}N.
\]
The proof rests on grouping the integers into blocks of length \(100\).

## 1. Integers with bounded digit sum have density zero

We first establish a quantitative bound for the number of integers having small digit sum.

For \(k,C\ge 0\), define
\[
W_k(C)=\#\{0\le q<10^k:S(q)\le C\}.
\]
We claim that
\[
W_k(C)\le (k+1)^C. \tag{1}
\]

We use the elementary decimal identity
\[
S(10q+d)=S(q)+d\qquad(0\le d<10). \tag{2}
\]
More generally, if \(0\le i<10^k\) and \(0\le j<10\), then
\[
S(10^k j+i)=j+S(i). \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, (3) follows by repeatedly applying (2), or equivalently by observing that multiplication by \(10^k\) appends \(k\) zeros and that the number \(i<10^k\) occupies only those final \(k\) digit positions.

We prove (1) by induction on \(k\). For \(k=0\), the only integer below \(10^0=1\) is \(0\), whose digit sum is \(0\), so \(W_0(C)=1=(0+1)^C\).

Suppose the estimate holds for \(k\). Every integer below \(10^{k+1}\) can be written uniquely as
\[
10^k j+i,
\qquad 0\le j<10,
\qquad 0\le i<10^k.
\]
By (3), if its digit sum is at most \(C\), then \(j\le C\) and \(S(i)\le C-j\). Hence
\[
W_{k+1}(C)
\le \sum_{j=0}^{C}W_k(C-j)
\le \sum_{j=0}^{C}(k+1)^{C-j}. \tag{4}
\]
Terms with \(j\ge10\), if any, merely enlarge the sum and therefore cause no problem.

The elementary polynomial estimate
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{C}(k+1)^{C-j}\le(k+2)^C \tag{5}
\]
completes the induction. For completeness, (5) itself follows by induction on \(C\). It is immediate for \(C=0\). If it holds for \(C\), then the corresponding sum for \(C+1\) is
\[
(k+1)^{C+1}+
\sum_{j=0}^{C}(k+1)^{C-j}
\le (k+1)^{C+1}+(k+2)^C.
\]
Since \((k+1)^C\le(k+2)^C\), the last expression is at most
\[
(k+1)(k+2)^C+(k+2)^C=(k+2)^{C+1}.
\]
Thus (1) is proved.

We now deduce the density-zero statement that will be needed below. Put
\[
E_C(N)=\#\{0\le q<N:S(q)\le C\}.
\]
If \(\ell(N)\) is the number of decimal digits of \(N\), then \(N<10^{\ell(N)}\), so (1) gives
\[
E_C(N)\le (\ell(N)+1)^C. \tag{6}
\]
For positive \(N\), the usual bounds associated with decimal length give
\[
10^{\ell(N)-1}\le N<10^{\ell(N)},
\]
and consequently
\[
\frac{(\ell(N)+1)^C}{N}
\le 10\frac{(\ell(N)+1)^C}{10^{\ell(N)}}. \tag{7}
\]
For fixed \(C\), a polynomial in \(\ell(N)\) divided by \(10^{\ell(N)}\) tends to zero. Also \(\ell(N)\to\infty\) as \(N\to\infty\). From (6) and (7),
\[
\frac{E_C(N)}N\longrightarrow0. \tag{8}
\]
Thus, for every fixed \(C\), the integers whose decimal digit sum is at most \(C\) form a set of asymptotic density zero.

## 2. Analysis of a block of one hundred consecutive integers

Fix a prefix \(q\), and consider numbers
\[
n=100q+d,\qquad 0\le d<100.
\]
We first analyze \(0\le d<99\); the final value \(d=99\) will be left untreated.
Write
\[
t=\left\lfloor\frac d{10}\right\rfloor,
\qquad u=d\bmod10,
\]
so that \(d=10t+u\), with \(0\le u<10\). Because \(d<99\), if \(u=9\) then \(t\le8\).

By the decimal digit-sum identity,
\[
S(100q+d)=S(q)+t+u. \tag{9}
\]
There are two cases.

### Case 1: \(u\ne9\)

There is no carry from the units digit when one is added. Therefore
\[
S(100q+d+1)=S(q)+t+u+1.
\]
The numerator in the definition of \(a(n)\) is strictly smaller than the denominator, so
\[
a(100q+d)=S(q)+t+u. \tag{10}
\]

### Case 2: \(u=9\)

Adding one changes the final decimal digits from \(t9\) to \((t+1)0\). Since \(t\le8\), there is no further carry into the digits of \(q\). Hence
\[
S(100q+d+1)=S(q)+t+1.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
S(100q+d)=S(q)+t+9=(S(q)+t+1)+8.
\]
Reduction modulo \(S(q)+t+1\) therefore gives
\[
a(100q+d)=8\bmod(S(q)+t+1). \tag{11}
\]

Now fix a threshold \(C\ge8\), and suppose that
\[
S(q)>C. \tag{12}
\]
Then the modulus in (11) is greater than \(8\), so (11) simplifies to
\[
a(100q+d)=8
\]
whenever
\[
d\in\{9,19,29,39,49,59,69,79,89\}. \tag{13}
\]
These are nine distinct positions in the block. Consequently, every complete block with \(S(q)>C\) contains at least nine occurrences of the value \(8\).

Next fix \(m\ne8\) and suppose in addition that \(m\le C\). For every \(d<99\), the value \(a(100q+d)\) cannot equal \(m\). Indeed, if \(d\bmod10=9\), it equals \(8\) by (11), whereas if \(d\bmod10\ne9\), equation (10) and (12) give
\[
a(100q+d)=S(q)+t+u>S(q)>C\ge m.
\]
Thus among the first \(99\) positions of such a block there are no occurrences of \(m\). The only position not covered by the analysis is \(d=99\), so the entire block contains at most one occurrence of \(m\). We have proved the key block estimates:

* if \(C\ge8\) and \(S(q)>C\), a complete block \(100q,\ldots,100q+99\) contains at least nine occurrences of \(8\);
* if also \(m\le C\) and \(m\ne8\), that block contains at most one occurrence of \(m\).

No claim about a block with \(S(q)\le C\) is needed; such prefixes will be the density-zero exceptional set from (8).

## 3. Global counting bounds

Fix \(m\ne8\), and choose
\[
C=\max\{m,8\}. \tag{14}
\]
Thus both \(m\le C\) and \(8\le C\).

Partition the integers \(0\le n<N\) according to
\[
q=\left\lfloor\frac n{100}\right\rfloor.
\]
The possible values of \(q\) are among
\[
0,1,\ldots,\left\lfloor\frac N{100}\right\rfloor,
\]
so there are at most
\[
K_N=\left\lfloor\frac N{100}\right\rfloor+1 \tag{15}
\]
such blocks, including a possible final incomplete block. Each block contains at most \(100\) integers below \(N\).

If \(S(q)>C\), the block estimate above shows that at most one of those integers can have value \(m\). If \(S(q)\le C\), we use only the trivial upper bound \(100\). It follows that
\[
A_m(N)
\le K_N+100E_C(K_N). \tag{16}
\]
This is slightly wasteful, since the baseline contribution of one has already been included for an exceptional block, but the stated bound is sufficient.

For the value \(8\), consider only complete blocks. There are
\[
L_N=\left\lfloor\frac N{100}\right\rfloor \tag{17}
\]
of them: for every \(q<L_N\), the entire interval from \(100q\) through \(100q+99\) lies below \(N\). Every such block with \(S(q)>C\) contributes at least nine occurrences of \(8\), while exceptional blocks contribute a nonnegative number. Hence
\[
A_8(N)
\ge 9\bigl(L_N-E_C(L_N)\bigr). \tag{18}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
A_8(N)\ge9L_N-9E_C(L_N). \tag{19}
\]
Here \(E_C(L_N)\le L_N\), so the right side is nonnegative.

## 4. Asymptotics of the bounds

First,
\[
\frac{\lfloor N/100\rfloor}{N}\longrightarrow\frac1{100}. \tag{20}
\]
For example, for positive \(N\),
\[
\frac1{100}-\frac1N
\le \frac{\lfloor N/100\rfloor}{N}
\le\frac1{100},
\]
which proves (20) by squeezing. It also follows that
\[
\frac{K_N}{N}
=
\frac{\lfloor N/100\rfloor+1}{N}
\longrightarrow\frac1{100}. \tag{21}
\]

By (8), the exceptional-prefix count is negligible. More explicitly, for all sufficiently large \(N\), \(K_N\le N\), and monotonicity of \(E_C\) gives
\[
0\le\frac{E_C(K_N)}N\le\frac{E_C(N)}N\longrightarrow0. \tag{22}
\]
Likewise, since \(L_N\le N\),
\[
0\le\frac{E_C(L_N)}N\le\frac{E_C(N)}N\longrightarrow0. \tag{23}
\]

Dividing (16) by \(N\), and using (21) and (22), shows that its right-hand side tends to \(1/100\):
\[
\frac{K_N+100E_C(K_N)}N
\longrightarrow\frac1{100}. \tag{24}
\]
Therefore
\[
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{A_m(N)}N\le\frac1{100}
\qquad(m\ne8). \tag{25}
\]
This passage to limsup is legitimate because the pointwise upper comparison (16) holds for every \(N\), the comparison sequence converges, and the frequency sequence is bounded between \(0\) and \(1\).

Similarly, dividing (19) by \(N\), and using (20) and (23), yields
\[
\frac{9L_N-9E_C(L_N)}N
\longrightarrow\frac9{100}. \tag{26}
\]
Since this expression is a pointwise lower bound for \(A_8(N)/N\), we obtain
\[
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{A_8(N)}N\ge\frac9{100}. \tag{27}
\]
Again, this follows from the standard monotonicity of limsup under pointwise comparison, together with convergence of the lower comparison sequence. Notice that for the lower bound we may simply take \(C=8\); (18) then counts the blocks whose prefix digit sum exceeds \(8\).

## 5. Final comparison

If \(m=8\), the two limsups in the desired inequality are identical. If \(m\ne8\), equations (25) and (27) give
\[
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{A_m(N)}N
\le\frac1{100}
\le\frac9{100}
\le
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{A_8(N)}N.
\]
Thus in every case
\[
\boxed{
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{A_8(N)}N
\ge
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{A_m(N)}N
}
\]
for every nonnegative integer \(m\), as required.
